short: Making a plan for how the money you expect to earn each month will be split between spending and saving.
kid: Before the school fair, you decide how many of your coins go on rides, how many on sweets and how many stay in your piggy bank. That way you don't run out halfway through.
detail: Budgeting is planning income against spending and saving over a period, usually a month. You start from take-home income, subtract fixed commitments such as rent, EMIs and insurance premiums, set limits for variable spending like food, travel and shopping, and assign a fixed amount to savings and investments, ideally moved out on payday, an approach called paying yourself first. Comparing actual spending with the plan shows where money leaks. Popular methods include the 50-30-20 rule, zero-based budgeting, where every rupee is given a job, and envelope budgeting; UPI apps and bank statements make tracking easy in India. Budgeting matters because emergency funds, investment plans and loan decisions all depend on a reliable monthly surplus. The common confusion: budgeting is not about cutting all spending, it is about choosing deliberately so money goes to what you value most.
example: Say Riya takes home ₹60,000 a month. She plans ₹20,000 for rent, ₹12,000 for food and transport, ₹8,000 for bills and her phone, ₹8,000 for eating out and shopping, and ₹12,000 for investments and her emergency fund. The plan adds up to exactly ₹60,000, so every rupee has a job.
formula: Monthly surplus = Take-home income - (Fixed costs + Variable spending)

short: Money kept aside in a safe, easy-to-reach place to pay for surprises like losing a job, an illness or an urgent repair.
kid: An emergency fund is a special jar of coins you never use for treats. If your bike breaks or you lose your lunch money, the jar is there to help.
detail: An emergency fund is a cash reserve set aside only for unplanned, essential costs: a job loss, a medical bill that insurance does not fully cover, an urgent home or vehicle repair, or helping family. The usual guideline is three to six months of essential expenses, and more for people with irregular income, a single earner in the family or dependants. The money must be safe and quickly available, so it is usually kept in a savings account, a sweep-in fixed deposit or a liquid mutual fund, not in shares that might be down just when it is needed. An emergency fund stops a shock from turning into expensive credit card or personal loan debt, and lets long-term investments stay invested. The common confusion: it is not an investment meant to earn high returns, and it does not replace health or term insurance.
example: Say Arjun's essential monthly costs, covering rent, food, EMIs, bills and insurance, come to ₹40,000. A six-month emergency fund is ₹40,000 x 6 = ₹2.4 lakh. If he saves ₹20,000 a month towards it, he reaches the target in 12 months.
formula: Emergency fund target = Monthly essential expenses x Number of months (commonly 3 to 6)

short: A simple budgeting guide: spend about half your take-home pay on needs, 30% on wants, and put 20% into savings and debt repayment.
kid: When you get ten sweets, you keep five for the lunch you really need, enjoy three as treats, and save two in your jar for later.
detail: The 50-30-20 rule splits after-tax income into three buckets: 50% for needs such as rent, groceries, utilities, insurance and minimum loan payments; 30% for wants such as eating out, travel, gadgets and subscriptions; and 20% for savings, investments and extra debt repayment. It was popularised by Elizabeth Warren, later a US senator, and her daughter Amelia Warren Tyagi in their 2005 book All Your Worth. Its strength is simplicity: it gives a first-time budgeter a starting point without tracking every rupee. It is a guideline, not a law. In high-rent Indian cities needs can take 60% or more of pay, while a young earner living with family might save 40% or more, and many planners argue that the savings share should rise with income. The common confusion: the percentages apply to take-home pay, not to CTC or gross salary.
example: Say Neha's take-home pay is ₹80,000 a month. Under the rule she would plan ₹40,000 for needs, ₹24,000 for wants and ₹16,000 for savings and investments, which together add back to ₹80,000.
formula: Needs = 50% x Take-home pay; Wants = 30% x Take-home pay; Savings and debt repayment = 20% x Take-home pay

short: What you own minus what you owe: the value of your savings, investments and property after subtracting all your loans and unpaid bills.
kid: Count all your toys and coins, then take away the ones you borrowed from friends. What is left that is truly yours shows how much you really have.
detail: Net worth is the total value of everything a person owns, their assets, minus everything they owe, their liabilities. Assets include bank balances, fixed deposits, mutual funds, shares, EPF and PPF balances, gold, property and vehicles, counted at current value. Liabilities include the outstanding home loan, car loan, personal loans and credit card dues. Net worth is a snapshot on one date, unlike income, which is a flow over time, so a high earner with big loans can have a low or even negative net worth. Tracking it yearly shows whether your finances are improving. For companies the same idea is shareholders' equity, which Indian filings and news also call net worth, as in a firm with negative net worth. Rich lists rank people by estimated net worth, mostly the market value of their shareholdings. The common confusion: net worth is not salary or cash in hand.
example: Say Kabir has ₹3 lakh in the bank, ₹5 lakh in mutual funds, ₹2 lakh in EPF and a flat worth ₹60 lakh, so his assets total ₹70 lakh. He owes ₹45 lakh on his home loan and ₹1 lakh on a credit card. His net worth is ₹70 lakh - ₹46 lakh = ₹24 lakh.
formula: Net worth = Total assets - Total liabilities

short: A quick shortcut for estimating how many years money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly growth rate in percent.
kid: It is a quick trick for guessing how long it takes your pile of marbles to become two piles, if it keeps growing a little bit every year.
detail: The rule of 72 estimates the doubling time of an amount growing at a steady compound rate: years to double are roughly 72 divided by the annual rate in percent. It works because the exact answer depends on the natural log of 2, about 0.693; 72 is used instead of 69.3 because it is close and divides neatly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, and it is most accurate for rates of about 6% to 10%. The rule of 70, or 69.3 for continuous compounding, gives similar answers and is common in economics: an economy growing 7% a year doubles its output in about 10 years. It also works in reverse for inflation: at 6% inflation, prices double, and money's buying power halves, in about 12 years. The common confusion: the rule assumes compound growth at a constant rate; it does not apply to simple interest.
example: At 8% a year compounded annually, the rule says money doubles in 72 / 8 = 9 years, so ₹1 lakh becomes about ₹2 lakh; the exact figure is ₹1 lakh x 1.08^9 = ₹1,99,900. At 12% the rule gives 6 years, against an exact answer of about 6.1 years.
formula: Years to double ≈ 72 / Annual rate (in %); exact: n = ln 2 / ln(1 + r)

short: Interest worked out only on the original amount lent or invested, never on interest already earned.
kid: You lend a friend five marbles, and every week they give you one extra marble as a thank-you. The thank-you never grows; it is always just one marble.
detail: Simple interest is interest calculated on the principal alone, at a fixed rate for each period, so SI = P x r x t. Because earned interest is not added back to the principal, the total grows in a straight line rather than exponentially. It is used for short-term calculations such as interest on some short loans, accrued interest on a bond between coupon dates and money-market yields. Over any period longer than one compounding interval, simple interest gives less than compound interest at the same rate, and the gap widens with time and with the rate. The common confusion is with flat-rate loans, offered by some lenders for vehicles and consumer goods: interest is charged on the original loan amount for the whole tenure even though you repay it every month, so a flat rate costs far more than the same reducing-balance rate.
example: ₹1 lakh invested at 8% simple interest for 3 years earns ₹1,00,000 x 0.08 x 3 = ₹24,000, so it grows to ₹1,24,000. With annual compounding it would grow to ₹1,25,971, because each year's interest also earns interest.
formula: SI = P x r x t; Amount = P x (1 + r x t), where P is principal, r the yearly rate and t the time in years

short: Interest earned on your original money and also on the interest it has already earned, so the total grows faster each period.
kid: Plant one seed and it grows a plant with more seeds. Plant those too, and soon you have a garden that keeps getting bigger faster.
detail: Compound interest is interest calculated on the principal plus all interest added in earlier periods. After t years the amount is A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where n is the number of compounding periods a year; more frequent compounding, quarterly, monthly or daily, gives a slightly higher effective annual rate. Indian bank fixed deposits usually compound quarterly, while PPF interest compounds yearly. Over long periods the effect is large because growth is exponential, which is why starting early matters more than investing large sums late. The same mechanism works against borrowers: unpaid credit card dues compound monthly at high rates. The common confusion: a quoted nominal rate is not the effective annual rate when compounding happens more than once a year; 12% compounded monthly works out to about 12.68% a year.
example: ₹1 lakh at 10% a year compounded annually grows to ₹1,00,000 x 1.1^3 = ₹1,33,100 after 3 years, against ₹1,30,000 with simple interest. After 20 years the compound amount is about ₹6.73 lakh, while simple interest would give ₹3 lakh.
formula: A = P x (1 + r/n)^(n x t); Compound interest = A - P

short: The yearly cost of a loan as a percentage, counting interest plus most fees and charges, so different loans can be compared fairly.
kid: Two shops sell the same toy. One has a smaller price tag but adds extra charges at the counter. This number tells you the real total, so you can pick the cheaper shop.
detail: The annual percentage rate (APR) is the annualised all-in cost of credit. It combines the interest rate with compulsory charges such as processing fees and insurance required as a condition of the loan, spread over the loan's life. A loan with a low headline rate but high fees can cost more than one with a higher rate and no fees, so APR allows fair comparison. In the US the Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose it. In India the RBI requires banks and NBFCs to give retail and MSME borrowers a Key Fact Statement showing the APR, under rules from October 2024. The common confusion: APR usually multiplies a periodic rate by the number of periods and ignores compounding within the year, so it can understate the effective annual rate; a card charging 3.5% a month has an APR of 42% but an effective rate of about 51%.
example: Say ABC Finance offers a one-year ₹1 lakh loan at 12%, repaid in a single payment, with a ₹2,000 processing fee deducted upfront. You actually receive ₹98,000 and repay ₹1,12,000, so the true cost is ₹14,000 on ₹98,000, an APR of about 14.3% rather than 12%.
formula: For a one-year, single-payment loan: APR = (Interest + Fees) / Amount actually received; in general, APR is the yearly rate at which the present value of all repayments equals the amount received

short: A bank deposit where you lock in a sum for a fixed period at an interest rate agreed upfront, with a penalty for withdrawing early.
kid: You give your piggy bank to a grown-up to keep safe for a whole year. You promise not to ask for it early, and when the year ends you get it back with a few extra coins.
detail: A fixed deposit (FD), called a term or time deposit in many countries, is money placed with a bank or a deposit-taking NBFC for a set tenure at a rate fixed on the day you open it. Interest is paid out or reinvested, and cumulative bank FDs usually compound quarterly. Breaking an FD early normally costs a penalty, often 0.5 to 1 percentage point off the rate. Bank FDs are insured by the DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, principal and interest together, under the rules as of 2025; corporate FDs from NBFCs are not insured and carry credit risk. Interest is taxed at your slab rate, with TDS above a threshold, so post-tax returns can trail inflation. FD rates follow the RBI's policy rate with a lag. The common confusion: an FD is risk-free only within the insured limit at a bank.
example: Say you put ₹1 lakh in a 2-year FD at 7% a year, compounded quarterly. Each quarter it grows by 1.75%, so after 8 quarters you receive ₹1,00,000 x 1.0175^8 = about ₹1,14,888.
formula: Maturity amount = P x (1 + r/4)^(4 x t), for quarterly compounding

short: A bank or post office deposit where you save the same amount every month for a set period, then get it back with interest.
kid: Every week you drop the same two coins into a special jar that stays shut. At the end, you get all your coins back plus a few bonus ones.
detail: A recurring deposit (RD) lets you save a fixed sum every month for a chosen tenure, typically 6 months to 10 years at banks and 5 years at India Post, at an interest rate locked in at the start. Each instalment earns interest only for the time it stays in the deposit, so the first instalment earns for the whole term and the last for a single month; banks usually compound quarterly. RDs suit people building a saving habit or saving for a known expense without market risk. Missing instalments can attract a penalty, and closing early usually lowers the rate. Interest is taxed at your slab rate, and bank RDs are subject to TDS. The common confusion: because each instalment is invested for a different length of time, total interest is roughly half of what the same rate would earn on the full amount for the whole term.
example: Say you deposit ₹5,000 a month for 12 months, putting in ₹60,000. Ignoring compounding, at 6% a year the first instalment earns for 12 months and the last for 1, an average of 6.5 months, so interest is ₹60,000 x 6% x 6.5/12 = ₹1,950 and you get back about ₹61,950.
formula: Interest (simple approximation) = Monthly instalment x (r/12) x n(n + 1)/2, where n is the number of months

short: A government-backed 15-year savings account in India with tax-free interest, into which you can deposit up to a yearly limit.
kid: It is a very safe money box looked after by the country. You keep adding coins for many years, and it slowly fills up with bonus coins you get to keep.
detail: The Public Provident Fund (PPF) is a long-term small savings scheme of the Government of India, offered through post offices and banks to resident individuals. Under the rules as of 2025 you can deposit between ₹500 and ₹1.5 lakh a financial year for a 15-year term, extendable in blocks of five years. The government sets the interest rate every quarter; interest is compounded yearly and, for each month, is earned on the lowest balance between the 5th and the month end, so early deposits earn more. PPF has exempt-exempt-exempt (EEE) status: deposits qualify for section 80C deduction under the old tax regime, and interest and maturity are tax-free. Partial withdrawals are allowed from the seventh financial year, and loans in the early years. It carries no default risk. The common confusion: PPF is open to any resident, salaried or not, and is separate from the EPF run through employers.
example: Say you deposit ₹1.5 lakh at the start of every year for 15 years at an assumed 7% a year. You put in ₹22.5 lakh and the account grows to about ₹40.3 lakh, all of it tax-free. The actual rate is reset every quarter, so the final figure will differ.
formula: Maturity value = Annual deposit x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r] x (1 + r), for deposits at the start of each year

short: India's compulsory retirement savings scheme for salaried workers, where employee and employer each put a share of salary into an interest-earning account.
kid: Every time you get pocket money, a little goes into a jar, and the grown-up who gives it adds about the same. You open the jar when you are old.
detail: The Employees' Provident Fund (EPF) is the main retirement savings scheme for India's organised sector, run by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) under the EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, now part of the Code on Social Security. It covers establishments with 20 or more workers. Under the rules as of 2025, the employee contributes 12% of basic pay plus dearness allowance; the employer also contributes 12%, but 8.33% of wages up to ₹15,000 a month goes to the Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS) and only the rest to EPF. The EPFO declares an interest rate every year, a closely watched figure for millions of savers. Each member has a Universal Account Number (UAN) that moves across jobs. Interest is largely tax-free, though, under the same rules, interest on employee contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year is taxable. The common confusion: EPF is employer-linked and compulsory, unlike the voluntary PPF.
example: Say your basic pay plus DA is ₹30,000 a month. You contribute 12%, or ₹3,600. Your employer also contributes ₹3,600, of which ₹1,250 (8.33% of the ₹15,000 wage ceiling) goes to EPS and ₹2,350 to EPF, so ₹5,950 a month lands in your EPF account under the rules as of 2025.
formula: Monthly EPF credit = 12% of (Basic + DA) from the employee + Employer's 12% minus the EPS share (8.33% of wages up to ₹15,000)

short: An optional extra amount a salaried worker can put into their own EPF account, above the compulsory 12%, earning the same interest rate.
kid: Besides the coins that go into your saving jar on their own, you can choose to drop in a few more of yours. They grow along with the rest.
detail: The Voluntary Provident Fund (VPF) is not a separate scheme but an option within EPF. An employee can ask the employer to deduct more than the compulsory 12% of basic pay plus dearness allowance, up to 100% of basic plus DA, and credit it to the same EPF account. The employer does not have to match the extra amount. VPF earns the EPF interest rate declared each year, which has generally been higher than bank fixed deposit rates, and shares EPF's government-backed safety. Contributions count towards the section 80C deduction under the old tax regime. Under the rules as of 2025, interest on total employee contributions, EPF plus VPF, above ₹2.5 lakh a year is taxable, which limits its appeal for high earners. The common confusion: VPF money follows EPF withdrawal rules, so it is meant for retirement, not short-term goals, and it is unrelated to PPF.
example: Say your basic pay plus DA is ₹50,000 a month. The compulsory 12% is ₹6,000; if you opt for another ₹4,000 as VPF, ₹10,000 a month is deducted from your salary, while your employer still contributes only its usual 12%, ₹6,000.
formula: Total employee contribution = 12% of (Basic + DA) + VPF amount

short: India's market-linked retirement savings scheme, regulated by PFRDA, where your contributions are invested in shares and bonds until you retire.
kid: You put a few coins in a special box every month, and helpers plant them so they grow. When you are very old, the box gives you a little money every month.
detail: The National Pension System (NPS) is a defined-contribution retirement scheme regulated by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA). Introduced in 2004 for new central government employees and opened to all citizens in 2009, it invests contributions through registered pension fund managers in equity, corporate bonds and government securities, chosen by the subscriber or automatically by age. The Tier I account is the locked retirement account; Tier II is an optional, withdrawable savings account. On exit, part of the corpus must buy an annuity that pays a monthly pension and the rest can be taken as a lump sum; PFRDA has relaxed the required split over time. Under the rules as of 2025, Tier I contributions earn an extra ₹50,000 deduction under section 80CCD(1B) in the old tax regime. The common confusion: NPS returns are not guaranteed, unlike EPF or PPF.
example: Say your Tier I corpus at 60 is ₹1 crore and you put 40% of it, the long-standing minimum, into an annuity. ₹40 lakh buys the pension and ₹60 lakh can be withdrawn as a lump sum; at an annuity rate of 6% a year, the ₹40 lakh pays ₹2.4 lakh a year, or ₹20,000 a month.

short: A government pension scheme for India's informal-sector workers that promises a fixed monthly pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 after age 60.
kid: A worker drops a few small coins into a box every month for many years. When they grow old, the box promises to give them the same little amount every month, no matter what.
detail: Atal Pension Yojana (APY) is a Government of India pension scheme launched in 2015 for workers in the unorganised sector, administered by PFRDA through the NPS system. Savers join between ages 18 and 40 through a bank or post office account and contribute a fixed amount monthly, quarterly or half-yearly until 60. In return the government guarantees a pension of ₹1,000, ₹2,000, ₹3,000, ₹4,000 or ₹5,000 a month from 60; if investment returns fall short, the government makes up the gap. After the subscriber's death the spouse receives the same pension, and after both, the nominee gets the accumulated corpus. The earlier one joins, the smaller the contribution. Since October 2022, income-tax payers cannot newly enrol. It matters as one of India's main tools for widening pension coverage among informal workers. The common confusion: APY pays a guaranteed fixed pension, unlike NPS, whose payout depends on markets.
example: Under the official contribution chart, someone joining at 18 pays ₹210 a month for 42 years to secure a ₹5,000 monthly pension, while someone joining at 40 pays ₹1,454 a month for 20 years for the same pension. The 18-year-old contributes about ₹1.06 lakh in total, against about ₹3.49 lakh for the 40-year-old.

short: A pension option for Indian central government employees, starting April 2025, that guarantees a monthly pension of up to half their recent basic pay.
kid: Some workers save a bit from every pay, and their boss adds more. When they stop working, they are promised a steady amount each month, about half of what they used to get.
detail: The Unified Pension Scheme (UPS) is an option within the National Pension System for central government employees, approved by the Union Cabinet in August 2024 and in force from 1 April 2025. Employees contribute 10% of basic pay plus dearness allowance and the government 18.5%, up from 14% under NPS, but the payout is assured: 50% of the average basic pay of the last 12 months for those with at least 25 years of service, proportionately less for 10 to 25 years, and at least ₹10,000 a month after 10 years. The pension rises with dearness relief, a spouse receives 60% of it as family pension, and a lump sum is paid at retirement. It matters for public finances because it brings back a guarantee whose cost falls on future budgets. The common confusion: UPS is not a return to the Old Pension Scheme, since employees still contribute.
example: Say a central government employee retires after 25 years with average basic pay of ₹80,000 a month over the last 12 months. The assured pension is 50% of that, ₹40,000 a month, plus dearness relief; with 15 years of service it would be 15/25 of that, or ₹24,000.
formula: Assured pension = 50% x Average basic pay of last 12 months x (Years of service / 25), for 10 to 25 years of service; minimum ₹10,000 a month with 10 or more years

short: A lump sum an employer pays a worker who leaves after long service, usually at least five years, as a reward for that service.
kid: When a helper has worked at your lemonade stand for a long, long time and finally leaves, you give them a big thank-you bag of coins. The longer they stayed, the bigger the bag.
detail: Gratuity is a one-time payment from an employer to an employee on retirement, resignation, death or disablement, rewarding long service. In India it was governed by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, now folded into the Code on Social Security, one of the labour codes in force since November 2025. It covers establishments with ten or more employees and needs five years of continuous service, waived on death or disablement; under the codes, fixed-term employees qualify after one year. It equals 15 days' wages, on a 26-day month, for each completed year of service, based on last drawn basic pay plus dearness allowance; a final part-year over six months counts as a full year. Under the rules as of 2025 the ceiling is ₹20 lakh, which is also the tax-free limit for private-sector employees. The common confusion: gratuity often appears in CTC, but it is paid only when you leave.
example: Say an employee leaves after 10 years and 7 months with last drawn basic pay plus DA of ₹52,000 a month. Service counts as 11 years, so gratuity is ₹52,000 x 15/26 x 11 = ₹3,30,000.
formula: Gratuity = Last drawn (Basic + DA) x 15/26 x Completed years of service

short: A government-backed savings scheme for Indians aged 60 and above that pays a fixed interest rate every quarter for five years.
kid: Grandma puts her savings in a very safe box. Every few months the box hands her a small, steady amount so she can buy what she needs.
detail: The Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme (SCSS) is a Government of India small savings scheme, offered through post offices and banks, for people aged 60 and above, with relaxations for some early and defence retirees. Under the rules as of 2025 an individual can invest up to ₹30 lakh; the account runs for five years and can be extended in three-year blocks. The government sets the rate every quarter, but once you invest it stays fixed for your deposit's term, and interest is paid out every quarter, making it a popular retirement income source. Deposits qualify for the section 80C deduction under the old tax regime, but the interest is fully taxable at slab rates and subject to TDS above a threshold. Being sovereign-backed, it carries no default risk. The common confusion: SCSS pays interest out instead of compounding it, so it suits income needs rather than long-term growth.
example: Say a retiree invests ₹30 lakh in SCSS at an assumed 8% a year. Interest is ₹30,00,000 x 8% = ₹2,40,000 a year, paid as ₹60,000 every quarter, and the ₹30 lakh is returned after five years.
formula: Quarterly interest = Deposit x Annual rate / 4

short: An Indian government savings scheme for a girl under 10, with tax-free interest, to build money for her education and future.
kid: When a baby girl is born, her family starts a special savings box just for her. They add coins for many years, and when she grows up the box is full to help her study.
detail: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY) is a small savings scheme launched by the Government of India in 2015 under the Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaign. Parents or guardians can open an account for a girl below 10, generally for up to two daughters. Under the rules as of 2025, deposits range from ₹250 to ₹1.5 lakh a financial year and are made for 15 years from opening; the account matures 21 years after opening. The rate is set quarterly, usually among the highest of the small savings schemes, and compounds yearly. SSY has exempt-exempt-exempt status: deposits qualify for section 80C under the old tax regime, and interest and maturity are tax-free. Up to 50% of the balance can be withdrawn for higher education once the girl turns 18 or passes Class 10. The common confusion: the account belongs to the girl, not the parent, and money cannot be withdrawn freely.
example: Say parents open an account at their daughter's birth and deposit ₹1.5 lakh at the start of each year for 15 years, ₹22.5 lakh in all. At an assumed 8% a year the balance reaches about ₹44 lakh by year 15 and, with no further deposits, about ₹69.8 lakh at maturity in year 21, all tax-free.

short: A five-year Indian government savings certificate sold at post offices that pays a fixed, compounded interest rate at maturity.
kid: You give the post office some coins and get a special paper. After five years you bring the paper back and get your coins plus extra ones.
detail: The National Savings Certificate (NSC) is a fixed-income small savings instrument issued by the Government of India and sold through post offices. The current series, NSC VIII Issue, has a five-year term; the government sets the rate every quarter, but it stays fixed for your certificate once bought. Interest compounds annually and is paid only at maturity, together with the principal. Under the rules as of 2025 the minimum investment is ₹1,000 with no upper limit. The amount invested qualifies for the section 80C deduction under the old tax regime, and so does each year's accrued interest except the last, because it is treated as reinvested. The interest itself is taxable, though no TDS is deducted. Certificates can be pledged as loan collateral, and early encashment is allowed only in limited cases such as the holder's death. The common confusion: NSC is not tax-free like PPF.
example: Say you buy an NSC for ₹1 lakh at an assumed 7.5% a year, compounded annually. After five years you receive ₹1,00,000 x 1.075^5 = about ₹1,43,563, of which ₹43,563 is interest.
formula: Maturity value = P x (1 + r)^5

short: Government-run savings products in India, such as PPF, NSC and Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme, offered through post offices and banks with rates set quarterly.
kid: The country runs a set of very safe piggy banks that anyone can use. Every few months it decides how many bonus coins each one gives.
detail: Small savings schemes are deposit products of the central government sold through India Post and authorised banks: the Public Provident Fund, National Savings Certificate, Kisan Vikas Patra, Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme, Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana, Post Office Monthly Income Scheme, and post office time and recurring deposits. They are sovereign-backed, so carry no default risk, and some offer tax benefits. The finance ministry resets their rates every quarter. Under a formula recommended by the Shyamala Gopinath committee in 2011, rates should track yields on government bonds of similar maturity plus a small spread, but the government often leaves them unchanged. Money collected goes into the National Small Savings Fund, which lends to the centre and finances part of the fiscal deficit. The rates matter for banks too, because attractive small savings rates compete for deposits. The common confusion: these are not bank FDs; the bank only acts as the government's agent.
example: Say the government sets a five-year NSC rate of 7% for a quarter. Anyone who buys in that quarter locks in 7%, so ₹1 lakh becomes ₹1,00,000 x 1.07^5 = about ₹1,40,255 at maturity, even if the rate is cut the next quarter.
formula: Formula rate (Gopinath committee) = Average yield on government bonds of similar maturity + Spread (0 to 1 percentage point, depending on the scheme)

short: Working out how much money you will need to live on after you stop working, then saving and investing steadily to build it.
kid: One day you will be too old to run the lemonade stand. So every summer you hide away a few coins, so there is enough for treats when you can't work anymore.
detail: Retirement planning is estimating the income you will need after you stop working and building the savings, or corpus, to pay for it. The steps are: project yearly expenses at retirement after inflation; estimate how long the money must last, often 25 to 30 years or more; work out the corpus needed; and set a monthly saving and asset-allocation plan to reach it. In India the building blocks include EPF, PPF, NPS and mutual funds, plus defined-benefit pensions for some government staff. A common rule of thumb is a corpus of 25 to 33 times the first year's expenses, linked to the 3-4% safe withdrawal rates found in US research. Inflation is the biggest threat: at 6% a year, costs double in about 12 years. The common confusion: retirement planning is not only for older people; starting in your twenties lets compounding do most of the work.
example: Say you spend ₹50,000 a month today and will retire in 30 years. At 6% inflation that becomes ₹50,000 x 1.06^30 = about ₹2.87 lakh a month, or about ₹34.5 lakh a year. Using a 25-times rule of thumb, the corpus needed is about ₹8.6 crore.
formula: Corpus needed ≈ First-year retirement expenses x 25 (to 33)

short: A goal of saving and investing a very large share of income so you no longer need a job, long before the usual retirement age.
kid: Some people save most of their pocket money instead of spending it on sweets. After a while they have so much saved that they can play all day without doing chores for coins.
detail: The FIRE movement, short for financial independence, retire early, is a personal finance approach built on very high savings rates, often 50% to 70% of income, invested mostly in low-cost index funds until the portfolio can cover living costs indefinitely. Its ideas trace to the 1992 book Your Money or Your Life by Vicki Robin and Joe Dominguez and spread through blogs in the 2010s. The usual target, the FIRE number, is 25 times annual expenses, based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate from US studies by William Bengen in 1994 and the Trinity study in 1998. Variants include Lean FIRE, on minimal spending, Fat FIRE, on comfortable spending, and Coast FIRE, saving enough early that growth alone reaches the target. Indian planners often suggest 30 to 40 times because of higher inflation. The common confusion: retiring early usually means freedom to choose work, not never working again.
example: Say a couple spends ₹12 lakh a year. Their FIRE number at 25 times expenses is ₹3 crore, and withdrawing 4% of that, ₹12 lakh, would cover the first year. Using a more cautious 33 times, they would need ₹3.96 crore.
formula: FIRE number = Annual expenses x 25 (equivalent to a 4% withdrawal rate); Savings rate = Savings / Take-home pay

short: The total yearly amount an employer spends on an employee, including salary, allowances, retirement contributions, insurance and bonuses, not just what you receive.
kid: When you help at a bake sale, they give you some coins, put a few in your saving jar for later and buy you a snack. All of that together is what you cost them.
detail: Cost to company (CTC) is the total annual expense an employer incurs on an employee, and the figure usually quoted in Indian job offers. It typically includes basic pay, house rent allowance and other allowances, the employer's EPF contribution, gratuity provision, insurance premiums, meal benefits, and performance bonuses or variable pay, and sometimes joining bonuses and stock grants. Take-home pay is much lower, for two reasons: CTC includes items you never receive monthly, and your own EPF contribution, professional tax and income tax are deducted from salary. Variable pay depends on performance, and gratuity is paid only after five years of service. The common confusion: comparing offers on CTC alone is misleading; compare fixed pay, monthly take-home, and how much is variable or one-time. Globally the closest equivalent is total compensation.
example: Say ABC Ltd offers a ₹12 lakh CTC: ₹10 lakh fixed salary, ₹1 lakh performance bonus, ₹50,000 employer PF, ₹20,000 gratuity provision and ₹30,000 health insurance. Only the ₹10 lakh fixed salary, minus your own PF, professional tax and income tax, reaches your bank account month by month, and the bonus comes only if targets are met.
formula: CTC = Gross salary + Employer's PF contribution + Gratuity provision + Insurance and other benefits + Variable pay

short: The salary actually paid into your bank account after income tax, provident fund and other deductions are taken out.
kid: A grown-up promises you ten coins, but keeps two for your piggy bank and gives one to the school fund. The seven that land in your hand are what you really get to spend.
detail: Take-home pay, or in-hand salary, is what an employee actually receives after all deductions from gross salary. In India these usually include the employee's EPF contribution of 12% of basic pay plus DA, professional tax levied by some states, income tax deducted at source (TDS) based on the chosen tax regime and declared investments, and items such as loan recoveries or voluntary VPF contributions. It is the right number for budgeting, judging an affordable EMI and comparing job offers, because cost to company includes employer costs, bonuses and benefits never paid monthly. Take-home pay can change during the year as TDS is adjusted for investment proofs. The common confusion: a raise in CTC does not lift take-home pay by the same amount, because higher tax slabs and PF absorb part of it. Elsewhere the terms net pay and after-tax pay mean the same thing.
example: Say your monthly gross salary is ₹80,000 with basic pay of ₹32,000. Deductions are employee PF of ₹3,840 (12% of basic), professional tax of ₹200 and TDS of ₹6,000, so take-home pay is ₹80,000 - ₹10,040 = ₹69,960.
formula: Take-home pay = Gross salary - Employee PF - Professional tax - Income tax (TDS) - Other deductions

short: When your spending rises every time your income rises, so you never end up saving more even though you earn more.
kid: Every time you get more pocket money, you buy bigger sweets. So your piggy bank never gets any fuller, even though you have more coins.
detail: Lifestyle inflation, or lifestyle creep, is the tendency for spending to climb in step with income: a raise brings a bigger flat, a pricier phone, more eating out and upgraded travel, and yesterday's luxuries become today's fixed needs. It is not inflation in the economic sense of rising prices but a behavioural pattern. The danger is that the savings rate stays flat or falls even as income grows, delaying goals such as an emergency fund, a home down payment or retirement, and leaving high fixed costs. EMIs taken on for upgrades lock it in. A common defence is to save or invest a fixed share of every increment, say half, before adjusting your lifestyle, and to automate it by raising a SIP. The common confusion: spending more as you earn more is not bad in itself; the problem is when savings do not rise too.
example: Say Aman's take-home pay rises from ₹60,000 to ₹90,000 a month and his spending rises from ₹48,000 to ₹84,000. He earns ₹30,000 more but now saves only ₹6,000 a month instead of ₹12,000, so his savings rate falls from 20% to under 7%.
formula: Savings rate = (Take-home pay - Spending) / Take-home pay

short: A three-digit number, from 300 to 900 in India, that shows how reliably a person has repaid loans and credit cards in the past.
kid: If you always give back the toys you borrow, friends happily lend you more. This number is like a star chart showing how good you are at giving things back.
detail: A credit score is a number that sums up a person's credit history and estimates how likely they are to repay. In India it is produced by credit information companies such as TransUnion CIBIL, Experian, Equifax and CRIF High Mark on a 300 to 900 scale, with scores above about 750 generally seen as good; US FICO scores run from 300 to 850. The main inputs are repayment history, how much of available credit limits you use, the length of your credit history, the mix of secured and unsecured loans, and recent applications for credit. Lenders use it to approve and price loans, so a higher score can mean a lower rate. Checking your own score is a soft enquiry and does not lower it. The common confusion: a credit score rates individuals' borrowing behaviour; a credit rating, from agencies like CRISIL, grades companies and their bonds.
example: Say Priya and Rahul each apply for a ₹30 lakh, 20-year home loan. Priya's score is 790 and the bank offers 8.5%; Rahul's is 680 after two missed EMIs, and he is offered 9.5%. Rahul's EMI is about ₹27,964 against Priya's ₹26,035, about ₹1,929 more every month.

short: A company that collects records of people's and businesses' borrowing and repayments from lenders, and turns them into credit reports and scores.
kid: Imagine a teacher who keeps a notebook of which children give back borrowed crayons on time. Before lending you crayons, another child can ask the teacher what the notebook says.
detail: A credit bureau collects data from banks, NBFCs and card issuers on every borrower's loans, credit limits, repayments and defaults, compiles credit reports and calculates scores that lenders use to decide whether, and at what price, to lend. In India bureaus are licensed by the RBI as credit information companies under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. There are four: TransUnion CIBIL, the oldest, Experian, Equifax and CRIF High Mark, and regulated lenders must report to all of them. Under RBI rules as of 2025, lenders update data at least every fortnight, each borrower can get one free full credit report a year from every bureau, and slow complaint handling triggers compensation. In the US, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion dominate. The common confusion: bureaus do not approve or reject loans, lenders do; and CIBIL is a company, not the name of the score.
example: Say ABC Bank gets a ₹5 lakh personal loan application. It pulls the applicant's bureau report and sees two credit cards, a car loan with all 36 EMIs paid on time and a score of 780, so it approves the loan; the bank's enquiry is itself recorded on the report for other lenders to see.

short: A card that lets you buy now and pay the bank later, with no interest if you clear the full bill by the due date.
kid: It is like a promise card at the toy shop: you take the toy today and promise to bring the coins next week. If you are late, you owe extra coins.
detail: A credit card gives a revolving line of credit up to a set limit: you spend, receive a monthly statement, and must pay by the due date, usually 15 to 25 days later. Paying the full statement balance means no interest at all, an interest-free loan of up to about 50 days. Paying only part, such as the minimum amount due, means interest on the outstanding balance, in India usually from each transaction date, at rates that as of 2025 often run around 3-4% a month, or 36-48% a year, plus late fees and GST. Cash withdrawals attract interest from day one. Used well, cards earn rewards and build a credit score. Monthly RBI data on card spends and balances is watched as a sign of consumer demand and stress. The common confusion: a debit card spends your own money; a credit card spends the bank's.
example: Say your statement shows ₹50,000 due. Paying the full ₹50,000 by the due date costs no interest. Paying only ₹10,000 leaves ₹40,000, and interest at an assumed 3.5% a month on that is at least ₹1,400 for the month, plus ₹252 of GST, charged at 18% on the interest under the rules as of 2025.

short: How much of your total credit card limits you are currently using, as a percentage; lower use generally helps your credit score.
kid: If a friend lets you borrow up to ten crayons and you only ever take two, they trust you. If you always take all ten, they start to worry.
detail: The credit utilisation ratio is the outstanding balance on revolving credit, mainly credit cards, divided by the total credit limit. Credit bureaus treat it as a key signal: high utilisation suggests a borrower is stretched and leaning on credit, so it pulls the score down, while low utilisation, commonly below 30%, looks healthy. It is calculated on the balances lenders report, usually the statement balance, both per card and across all cards. Because it reflects only the latest reported balances, it can improve quickly once balances are paid down, unlike missed payments, which stay on the record for years. Ways to keep it low include paying before the statement date, spreading spending across cards, or a higher limit, though asking for one can trigger a hard enquiry. The common confusion: paying in full every month does not guarantee low utilisation if the reported statement balance is high.
example: Say you have two cards with limits of ₹1 lakh and ₹50,000, and statement balances of ₹30,000 and ₹15,000. Utilisation is ₹45,000 / ₹1,50,000 = 30%. Paying ₹30,000 before the statement dates brings it to ₹15,000 / ₹1,50,000 = 10%.
formula: Credit utilisation ratio = Total revolving balances / Total credit limits x 100

short: The smallest payment a credit card company accepts by the due date to avoid a late fee; interest is still charged on the unpaid balance.
kid: If you owe a friend ten sweets, giving back just one this week keeps them from getting cross. But you still owe the other nine, and they will ask for a few extra later.
detail: The minimum amount due is the lowest payment a credit card issuer requires by the due date to keep the account in good standing. In India it is often about 5% of the outstanding balance plus any EMIs, fees, interest and over-limit amount, though each issuer sets its own formula; RBI rules require it to be set so the balance is not left growing, known as no negative amortisation. Paying it avoids a late-payment fee and a missed-payment mark on your credit report, but you lose interest-free credit: interest is charged on the whole outstanding, usually from each transaction date, at rates that as of 2025 often exceed 40% a year. Paying only the minimum month after month can stretch repayment over years and multiply the total cost. The common confusion: the minimum due is a floor to avoid default, not a sensible repayment target.
example: Say your statement shows ₹40,000 outstanding and the minimum due is 5%, or ₹2,000. Paying ₹2,000 avoids the late fee, but interest at an assumed 3.5% a month on the remaining ₹38,000 is at least ₹1,330, so the debt shrinks by only ₹670 that month before GST and new purchases.
formula: Minimum amount due ≈ About 5% of outstanding balance + EMIs, fees, interest and any over-limit amount (varies by issuer)

short: A fixed amount a borrower pays every month to repay a loan, covering both interest and part of the original amount borrowed.
kid: You borrow ten sweets from a friend and give back the same small handful every week, plus a tiny extra as thanks, until you have paid them all back.
detail: An equated monthly instalment (EMI) is the fixed monthly payment that repays a loan, with interest, over an agreed tenure. Each EMI has two parts: interest on the outstanding balance and repayment of principal. Early EMIs are mostly interest; as the balance falls, the principal share rises, a pattern called amortisation. The EMI depends on the loan amount, interest rate and tenure, and a longer tenure lowers the EMI but raises total interest. In India most home loans have floating rates linked to an external benchmark such as the RBI repo rate, so when rates change lenders often adjust the tenure rather than the EMI, though borrowers can choose. No-cost EMI offers on gadgets usually build the interest into the price or offset it with a discount. The common confusion: a lower EMI is not a cheaper loan; total interest over the tenure is what counts.
example: A ₹10 lakh loan at 12% a year (1% a month) for 5 years has an EMI of about ₹22,244. Over 60 months the borrower pays about ₹13.35 lakh, so total interest is about ₹3.35 lakh; in the first month ₹10,000 of the EMI is interest and ₹12,244 repays principal.
formula: EMI = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1), where P is the loan amount, r the monthly interest rate and n the number of months

short: The share of your monthly income that already goes to loan repayments; lenders use it to judge how much more you can safely borrow.
kid: If you get ten coins a week and already owe friends six of them, there is not much left for anything else. Grown-ups check this before lending you more.
detail: The debt-to-income (DTI) ratio compares a borrower's regular debt payments with their income, usually per month. Indian lenders use the closely related fixed obligation to income ratio (FOIR), which divides all existing EMIs, card dues and other fixed obligations, plus the proposed new EMI, by monthly income, usually net income. Many lenders cap FOIR at roughly 40% to 60% depending on income and loan type, so even a borrower with a strong credit score may be offered a smaller loan if existing EMIs are high. In the US, mortgage lenders look at DTI on gross income, with 43% long a benchmark under the original qualified-mortgage rules. Regulators also track household debt-service ratios as a gauge of financial stability. The common confusion: DTI uses periodic payments, not the total amount of debt outstanding, so a large loan over a long tenure can still fit within the limit.
example: Say Meera's net monthly income is ₹1 lakh and she already pays a ₹20,000 car loan EMI. If her lender caps FOIR at 50%, her total EMIs can be ₹50,000 a month, so the largest new EMI she can take on is ₹30,000.
formula: DTI = Total monthly debt payments / Gross monthly income x 100; FOIR = (Existing EMIs + Proposed EMI + Other fixed obligations) / Monthly income x 100

short: A long-term loan from a bank or housing finance company to buy or build a home, with the home itself pledged as security.
kid: A house costs more coins than a family has. Someone lends them the rest, and the family pays back a little every month for many years while living in it.
detail: A home loan is a secured loan, usually for 15 to 30 years, to buy, build or renovate a home; the lender holds a mortgage on the property until it is repaid. Lenders finance only part of the value, capped by RBI loan-to-value limits, which as of 2025 allow up to 90% for loans up to ₹30 lakh and less for bigger loans, so the buyer pays the rest as a down payment. Most Indian home loans carry floating rates linked to an external benchmark, usually the repo rate, so policy rate changes pass through, and borrowers pay no prepayment penalty. Under the old tax regime as of 2025, interest of up to ₹2 lakh a year on a self-occupied home is deductible under section 24(b), and principal under section 80C. The common confusion: the EMI is not the only cost; fees, stamp duty and insurance add up.
example: Say you buy a flat for ₹60 lakh with a ₹48 lakh home loan, 80% of the price, paying ₹12 lakh as down payment. At 8.5% for 20 years the EMI is about ₹41,656, and over 240 months you repay about ₹1 crore, so roughly ₹52 lakh goes in interest.
formula: EMI = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1); Loan-to-value ratio = Loan amount / Property value

short: A loan for almost any purpose, from a medical bill to a wedding, given without pledging any asset, based on your income and credit history.
kid: A grown-up lends you coins without asking you to leave your favourite toy as a promise. Because they are trusting you more, they ask for more extra coins back.
detail: A personal loan is an unsecured term loan, usually for one to five years, that the borrower can use for any legitimate purpose: medical costs, weddings, travel, home repairs or paying off costlier card debt. With no collateral, lenders rely on income, employer, existing EMIs and credit score, and charge more than on home or car loans; as of 2025 rates commonly ran from about 10% to over 20% a year, plus processing fees. It is repaid in EMIs, and money can arrive within hours from digital lenders. Rapid growth in such loans led the RBI in November 2023 to raise risk weights on unsecured consumer credit, making it costlier for banks and NBFCs to lend. The common confusion: a pre-approved offer is not cheap money; compare the annual percentage rate including fees, and borrow to clear card debt only when the rate is lower.
example: Say you borrow ₹3 lakh at 14% a year for 3 years with a 2% processing fee. You receive ₹2,94,000 after the ₹6,000 fee, pay an EMI of about ₹10,253, and repay about ₹3.69 lakh in all.
formula: EMI = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
